analysis.investment_thesis: Campus Activewear trades at INR 248 against a computed Graham Number of ~INR 47 — more than 5× intrinsic value by my calculation — offering zero margin of safety. At P/E 55.7× and P/B 9.5×, the investor is paying entirely for speculative future growth, not proven earning power.
key_strengths: 7-year consecutive earnings record (2018–2025), satisfying my minimum track-record requirement
Interest coverage ratio ~9.6× (Operating Income INR 183 Cr ÷ Finance Cost INR 19 Cr) — debt is well-serviced
OCF positive all 5 years; FY2024–25 free cash flow of INR 176–219 Cr shows real cash generation
key_risks: Earnings are volatile, not stable — Net Profit swung from INR 117 Cr (2023) → 89 Cr (2024) → 121 Cr (2025); a business I trust must show monotonic progress
Consumer cyclical footwear is highly price-elastic; a demand slowdown compresses margins rapidly (Operating Income fell from INR 242 Cr in FY22 to INR 143 Cr in FY24)
No dividend yield disclosed — shareholders receive no cash return while paying a 55× earnings multiple
red_flags: Graham Number ≈ INR 47 (√22.5 × ~3.97 EPS × ~24.8 BVPS); current price INR 248 implies a 5.3× premium to intrinsic asset-backed value
P/B of 9.5× is more than 6× my ceiling of 1.5× — the entire market cap is a bet on brand intangibles, not tangible assets

No dividend history — management retains all earnings yet ROE has not compounded the book value proportionately (equity grew from INR 428 Cr to 757 Cr over 3 years, broadly in line with retained earnings, not exceptional reinvestment)
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Campus Activewear possesses a recognisable consumer brand and has grown revenue from INR 508 Cr (FY18) to INR 1,593 Cr (FY25), which is commendable. However, my method demands I pay for what a business has already proven, not what it might achieve. At P/E 55.7× and P/B 9.5×, the current price is entirely a projection of future growth — precisely the speculative posture I caution the defensive investor to avoid. The Graham Number of ~INR 47, derived from actual reported EPS (~INR 3.97) and book value per share (~INR 24.8), makes the overvaluation arithmetic inescapable. The debt-to-equity ratio of 0.48 is the one metric that approaches my comfort zone, and operating cash flow has been consistently positive, which I acknowledge.

What disturbs me most is the earnings instability. Net profit fell 57% from FY22 to FY21, then again 24% from FY23 to FY24 — a cyclical pattern inconsistent with the stable, predictable earning power I require before committing capital. An intelligent investor should demand compensation for this volatility through a low price, not pay a premium for it. Mr. Market, in his enthusiasm for the athleisure theme, is pricing this business as though growth is certain and perpetual. History teaches otherwise. I would revisit only if the price declined toward INR 50–70, offering a genuine margin of safety against proven book value.
